Signal requests that protection on your behalf. Google doesn’t currently offer any sort of similar option. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents. stories.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
stories.description: From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people. Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll . That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking. stories.title: Teachers want to prepare pupils for post-16 life. This is why it’s so difficult | Lola Okolosie
stories.description: I welcome Alan Milburn’s call for schools to focus more on students’ potential beyond exams. Yet I must ask: where is the money? At 16, life should feel like a path leading to endless opportunities. That is at least the carrot dangled in front of young people to motivate them through the gruelling years of exam preparation. “Your life starts now,” their teachers all but tell them. And though for the vast majority that is true, there is a cohort who are forced to accept that the bright futures they were promised are beyond their reach. They are the nearly one million young people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets). Alan Milburn’s second report on the nation’s Neets places schools at the heart of the solution. It proposes that schools should be judged not only on grades but also whether pupils continue their post-16 journey into further education or work. Technical education, it also argues, must be regarded with the same gravitas as the academic. Most people working in education won’t argue with this rationale. As ever, the sticking point is how it is to be funded. Lola Okolosie is an English teacher and writer Continue reading...

stories.title: Outage Chaos: When Tech is too Big to Fail
stories.description: Outages happen, but we deserve a resilient internet where no one outage at one company can put people at risk and disrupt the global economy. We can only get there by addressing an over-reliance on a few cloud monopolists through effective antitrust laws and interoperability requirements. Service outages, like we’ve seen recently at Microsoft , Apple *, banks , courts , airlines , and elsewhere, can be more than an annoying hurdle. Losing a vital service due to an error can cause the same impacts as a government-ordered internet shutdown—people losing access to vital information and lines of communication. As usual, the greatest harms are faced by people on the margins globally. There’s not much hope in companies out-nerding these issues either. Technical errors will always exist, whether it’s a bug , negligence from an administrator, or a malicious attack. The problem is an over-reliance on any one company or system when these inevitable outages occur. stories.title: Voters Reject ALPRs and Surveillance Tech at the Ballot Box
stories.description: Do automated license plate readers (ALPRs) have any place in our communities? That question has been a hot topic in city council meetings , community conversations , and news coverage around the country for months. This past election day, a couple of U.S communities took it further: to the ballot. And overwhelmingly, voters decided that, no, these devices should not be deployed on our streets. We agree! In Maine, the coastal community of York voted to remove the town’s existing ALPR cameras and require that any future proposed installations receive voter approval before proceeding. The local initiative ended up on the ballot after constituents gathered enough signatures on a citizens’ petition for a local ordinance. On Election Day, nearly three-quarters of York voters supported the ban. Thousands of miles away, voters in League City, Texas also voted against allowing the local police department to continue use of ALPR cameras. stories.title: The Justice Department Wants To Give Patent Trolls More Power
stories.description: Software patents are mostly vague, hard to define, and widely abused. Most tech patent lawsuits aren’t filed by companies that make real products. They’re filed by patent trolls, companies that acquire patents to extract payments through litigation and legal threats. A patent on one feature of a smartphone shouldn’t give the patent owner the power to threaten the existence of the entire product line. But that is exactly the leverage patent trolls want—and the current administration is helping them to get it. In two recent patent cases, Radian Memory Systems v. Samsung and Collision Communications v. Samsung, the Justice Department and the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office have asked courts to make it easier for patent owners to get injunctions. These are judicial orders that can force companies to stop selling products or remove features from them, rather than simply pay monetary damages. The threat of an injunction can pressure a company to pay far more than what a patent is actually worth. stories.title: The Paramount-Warner Brothers Deal Could Usher in Another Age of Lost Media
stories.description: There are all sorts of reasons to be against the merger of Paramount and Warner Brothers-Discovery. There's the obvious problem of increasing concentration in the already pretty-concentrated film and TV industry. People have problems with Paramount's owner Skydance interfering with its news coverage and late night comedy . But one of the biggest is the way we are losing choice and access to information and culture. In the context of the digital world, there are two major problems with these mega mergers. One, as we've said in the past, is that it further degrades the already awful state of mainstream streaming services. In short, by increasing the amount of legacy content under their control, major studios don't have to invest in either new content or well-engineered services to get users. Plus, they can pool the data they have on users together in an increasing assault on consumer privacy. A monthly subscription and more information about your habits and interests? Win-win for them.
